727	## Layer 6 — Data protection and prompt-injection defence
728	
729	**Principle.** The design keeps PHI from reaching the coding agent (owner decision, research 1.9).
730	Some paths rely on process (below), so this is a target, not a guarantee. Other customer
731	personal data is outside that hard boundary ("not extended", research 5.8): the agent reads metadata
732	by default and may read such data case by case under GĐ-9. Real-data reads are approved, name one
733	tenant, are time-boxed, and need an agreement (BAA/DPA, partner contract) (GĐ-9). Everything read
734	from outside is untrusted. Non-prod is synthetic or masked (GĐ-14).
735	
736	**On Papaya's stack**
737	
738	- **Paths to PHI** (research 1.11.4 lists 17):
739	  - AWS stores: closed by identity, through `ProdReadMetadata` as the only standing prod role from
740	    phase 1 (existing broad read roles are removed) and the SCP from phase 2
741	    (layer 1); no Aurora credentials, no prod exec, no `lambda:InvokeFunction` for agent-usable roles
742	    [design; actions ⚠️ G13];
743	  - k0s logs/exec and GCP stores (L1, L11, L13): same principle, mechanism open (G1, G3);
744	  - tickets/chat via MCP, pasted text, internal admin pages, prod AI traces, fixtures, CI logs (L5,
745	    L8–L10, L12, L14): process and hygiene only;
746	  - logs redacted at source with raw payloads in a separate log group; alerts carry IDs, not payloads [design].
747	    Redaction lives in application code, so one approved PR that logs a whole event would put
748	    PHI in a log group the agent reads. A second layer outside the code (OD28) [design]:
749	    - a CloudWatch Logs data protection policy on every log group `ProdReadMetadata` reads, set
750	      **before** the group is opened, because masking applies at ingestion only; masked data is
751	      hidden "at all egress points, including CloudWatch Logs Insights" (📖 R9.2.7);
752	    - custom identifiers keyed on field names (national ID, HKID, bank account, diagnosis,
753	      insured name; examples E14), because AWS has no managed identifier for Vietnam, Thailand
754	      or Hong Kong (📖 R9.2.8); at most 10, each regex ≤ 200 characters (📖 R9.2.9);
755	    - no agent-usable role holds `logs:Unmask`, and none gets `CloudWatchLogsFullAccess`, which
756	      includes it (📖 R9.2.7; E6 test);
757	    - a required SAST rule against logging whole events or payload objects in the claims
758	      services' handlers (S10; product open, G4); a log-level change already stops at the risk
759	      stop (`logging` property), because debug output can carry PHI.
760	    Limit: field-name masking catches structured logs, not free text in a message. It is a second
761	    layer; code review and the SAST rule remain the first. Cost: $0.12 per GB scanned
762	    (📖 R9.2.10) and masked values while debugging.
763	- **Real-data request** [design]: tenant, purpose, store, window, agreement; approved by the data owner
764	  and an approver ≠ requester; JIT data-read role, 1 h. At night the data owner is not on call: the
765	  on-call approver approves alone and the data owner reviews the grant the next working day. This
766	  applies to non-PHI and PHI alike; for PHI the reader is still a human without an agent. Per-tenant scoping through session tags
767	  (📖 R2.1.8) is unresolved, because tags come from user attributes (⚠️).
768	  - **PHI:** a human reads in a terminal without an agent (process rule, layer 1); the agent gets a
769	    redacted summary. This
770	    narrows GĐ-9 because the agent stays outside PHI scope (research 1.9) and Team is not shown as
771	    BAA-covered (⚠️ R1.11.3.4). Enterprise + BAA only for a separate environment if needed (research 1.9).
772	  - **Non-PHI personal data:** the agent may read it within the approved request (GĐ-9). Claim
773	    tables mix health, ID and bank data (research 1.11.4 L2), so a store that holds PHI is treated as
774	    PHI unless the agent reads a view or extract without PHI [design].
775	- **Partner-uploaded claim documents (A7b):** never in an agent session raw; reproduce with synthetic
776	  documents, or de-identify first [design]. The document is PHI and an injection vector (research
777	  1.11.4 L6).
778	- **Injection** (these lower frequency; layers 1 and 3 limit impact): Manual by default (sandboxed Bash runs without a prompt, layer 2); the auto-mode
779	  classifier missed 17 % of 52 real overeager actions and 5.7 % of 1,000 synthetic exfiltration
780	  attempts (📖 R6.3.5). Broad allowed domains such as `github.com` are a documented exfiltration path
781	  (📖 R6.3.7). The incident session has no WebFetch, likely no edit tools (layer 2), and runs outside
782	  the repo, but its Bash can still write locally and send data out through excluded
783	  commands (layer 2), including the SSO token cache; "no standing write, no PHI read" limits what
784	  the token opens, except during a JIT or data-read window (layer 2 mitigations). Shared knowledge
785	  goes in `CLAUDE.md` under review; auto memory is exempt from the protected-path rules unless `--restricted` (📖 R6.3.11, D3).
786	- **Tenants:** one tenant per data-read grant; a session that read one tenant's data does not post to
787	  shared places without review (⚠️ R6.5 #8, process). Logical separation in shared accounts is assumed
788	  (GĐ-3, unconfirmed).

793	  `cleanupPeriodDays` (30 in the HIPAA sample, 📖 R5.5.4; what it deletes ⚠️).

797	  sensitive (s.26) and a transfer abroad needs an adequate destination or a s.29 safeguard in the
798	  provider contract (📖 R9.7.1, R9.7.2); breaches go to the PDPC Office within 72 hours where
799	  feasible (📖 R9.7.3). Hong Kong: purpose limitation and processor contracts; breach notice is
800	  voluntary today (📖 R9.7.6, R9.7.8). Each tenant's profile and the breach row are in the
801	  compliance register (C-18, C-26); sector rules of the insurance regulators stay open (O-10, O-11).

813	
814	**Principle.** One tamper-evident evidence chain per prod change. One routed alert channel with a
815	named on-call, approvers included. Unapproved change is detected (drift, reconciliation). Break-glass
816	is approved before use, time-boxed and reconciled after.

821	  integrity validation (📖 R2.6.2, R2.6.4), data events only on PHI buckets, prod Lambda invoke and
822	  prod SQS; an **evidence bucket** with Object Lock in compliance mode for 6 years (📖 R9.2.12),
823	  filled nightly with merged PRs, reviews, checks and deploy logs (examples E13) and monthly with

856	
857	  | Step | Rule |
858	  |---|---|
859	  | When | Only during an incident (Options §9 Q2), when the PR path cannot be used: operation not in IaC and no runbook; GitHub/Actions down; pipeline broken. The approver refuses JIT for anything expressible in IaC while the pipeline works, and records why. Outside incidents, an operation not in IaC waits for IaC or a runbook. |
860	  | Request | Command list, scope, reason, incident link, in a channel that does not depend on GitHub. |
861	  | Approval | On-call approver ≠ requester, before the grant (Options §4b; OD7; backup rule OD2). The approver moves the Linear request to "Approved"; a receiver in the tooling account (next to the approval-gate app) gets the signed webhook (📖 [Linear webhooks](https://linear.app/developers/webhooks): HMAC-SHA256 `Linear-Signature`, `actor`, `updatedFrom`) and grants only if the signature is valid and fresh, a person made the change, the approver ≠ the requester as Identity Center users (people register, OD25), the approver is on shift, the incident is open and the permission set is an allowed `InfraOperator-*` (OD33; examples E16). One grant per request: a retried webhook or a second move to "Approved" grants nothing (Linear retries up to 3 times, 📖 same page). The receiver's role may assign only permission sets tagged `jit-grant`, in the prod accounts, and may never create, change or re-tag a permission set (examples E16; resource types ✅ AWS Service Reference). Linear accounts sign in through single sign-on and are in the people register (Linear plan for SSO ⚠️ not checked). The AWS TEAM sample is compared with the receiver before building it (rollout 1.13). If the receiver is down, an L3 owner team member grants by hand against the same checklist; the Identity Center alert (layer 1) fires on it and the monthly report reviews it. |
862	  | Grant | `InfraOperator-<service>`; role session 1 h (📖 R2.1.4). Deleting the assignment likely stops only new sessions (⚠️ R2.4.2, R2.9 #3), so the real window can approach 2 h; ending the portal session does not end role sessions (📖 R2.4.3). An immediate stop needs the revocation SCP, which must keep the user blocked for at least 12 h (📖 R2.4.4). Applying it is a management-account change held by the L3 owner team only, and no night-time path for it is designed yet (⚠️ G20): until one exists, a misused grant may run to the end of its window. Candidate: a pre-approved revocation runbook for one named L3 owner reachable by phone, or an org-wide `aws:TokenIssueTime` Deny as kill switch (⚠️ R2.9 #3). |
863	  | Execution | The grant goes to the requester (the incident responder), who types the commands; no agent in that terminal (D2). D2 said the on-call person runs them; OD7 moves that to the responder, since on-call engineers only approve. |
864	  | After | A job compares CloudTrail writes in the window with the list; a codify PR within a fixed deadline (as soon as GitHub is back); drift detection until it merges. |
865	  | Identity Center outage | Emergency SAML federation to roles, built and tested in advance (📖 R2.1.11; ⚠️ R2.9 #2); no user mapped until an approved activation, which is alerted. |

883	
884	**Cost / value.** The incident lane is slower than direct access (estimated 11–46 vs 2–20 min,
885	Options §6), and JIT needs a written command list. Compliance gets approval before apply even in
886	incidents, plus detection.
887	
888	---
889	
890	## Layer 8 — Governance and rollout
891	
892	**Principle.** Every control has an owner, a metric and a review date. Policies are files changed by
893	PR. Access is never removed before its replacement works. Controls are tested against realistic
894	attacks.
895	
896	**On Papaya's stack**
897	
898	- **Owners:** DevSecOps (framework, managed settings, catalogue, metrics); a platform team or named
899	  engineers (deploy workflows, rulesets, pipelines; whether Papaya has a platform team is unknown ⚠️); Compliance (evidence review, supplier register, Statement of
900	  Applicability); engineering leads (decide CODEOWNERS content; changes to it are approved by the L3 owner team); engineering management (on-call schedule).
901	- **Policy as code:** catalogue, SCPs, trust policies, CODEOWNERS and workflows are files under
902	  CODEOWNERS. Settings that live outside files are kept as an expected copy in git and compared with
903	  the live state: GitHub settings (⚠️ R3.6 #1; G8) and Claude managed settings, which are edited in
904	  the admin console (📖 R1.1.5; comparison method in layer 2). Few GitHub admins and Claude org
905	  Owners, reviewed quarterly.
906	- **Metrics:** S1–S11 exactly as in framing §5; this framework adds the JIT metrics (layer 7) and the
907	  prompt metrics (layer 2). S2 and S5 have caveats (OD1; layer 2).
908	- **Rollout** (≈ 100 days, re-baselined from GĐ-12's 90 after the effort estimate, OD49): [`03-rollout-plan.md`](03-rollout-plan.md), moved
909	  there with its items unchanged except syncs with the examples' findings (trail deny, allowlist,
910	  phase-2 version floor), and expanded with owners and checks [design]. Order (framing Q8): (1) remove long-lived CI credentials, (2) narrow standing prod
911	  access, (3) MCP/plugin catalogue; the on-call approver list before or with (2). Phase 1 (days 0–45)
912	  makes the PR the default prod write path, with eight hard prerequisites before standing prod write is
913	  removed; phase 2 (45–75) adds SCPs, the rest of the managed baseline and automated
914	  reconciliation; phase 3 (75–100) tests and reviews. The phase-1 load is the main rollout risk: a
915	  rough estimate (⚠️) is 75–110 person-days, so the rollout plan names a minimum safe phase 1 for 2
916	  DevSecOps people and one platform engineer over about 45 days, and a degraded mode if the
917	  approval-gate app is late (OD35).
918	
919	- **Exceptions:** a ticket with owner, reason and expiry.
920	- **Standards mapping:** ISO 27001:2022 Annex A (IDs recalled, ⚠️ R5.1), HIPAA Security Rule
921	  (📖 R5.2) and Vietnam law (📖 R5.4) are mapped per control area in the
922	  [compliance register](04-compliance-mapping.md#standards-cross-reference), with every caveat. "A named human approves"
923	  is Papaya's chosen way to meet these controls, not a literal requirement (⚠️ R5.7 #1).
924	- **Out of scope:** security of the production AI agents (A7a); noted as a follow-up.
925	
926	**Audit evidence.** Git history of policy files, monthly metrics, 90-day review minutes, the exception register and planted-injection reports; standards: [04-compliance-mapping.md](04-compliance-mapping.md#standards-cross-reference).
927	
928	**Cost / value.** Steady, small overhead for DevSecOps and the owners of deploy workflows. Compliance gets a managed system
929	with owners and review dates.
930	
931	---
932	
933	## Gaps and the author's decisions
934	
935	Twenty gaps (G1–G20: not designed, or only an open item) and the author's design decisions
936	(OD1–OD52) are in the appendix: [gaps](07-framework-appendix.md#q-gaps),
937	[decisions](07-framework-appendix.md#r-authors-design-decisions-od-n-2026-11-09).

1	     1	# Engineer guide: working with Claude Code at Papaya
2	     2	
3	     3	> Status: a summary of the approved framework; it adds no rule · Updated: 2026-11-09 · Builds on
4	     4	> [`01-framework.md`](01-framework.md)
5	     5	
6	     6	This page answers one question: **what changes in my working day?** Each section says what you do,
7	     7	who approves, and how long it takes. The rules and their sources are in the framework layer linked
8	     8	from each section; if this page and the framework differ, the framework wins. Times are targets from
9	     9	the success criteria (S-n) or estimates marked ⚠️.
10	    10	
11	    11	## The short version
12	    12	
13	    13	- **Non-prod is yours.** Build, deploy and debug in non-prod with the agent, with no new approval (S4),
14	    14	  once a store has been scanned for real data (until then it follows the real-data rule, section 5).
15	    15	- **Prod reads are metrics and metadata.** No standing prod write for anyone, you included.
16	    16	- **Every prod change is a pull request.** One code owner who is not you approves; CI applies it.
17	    17	- **In an incident the path is the same, with faster people:** an on-call approver, 24/7.
18	    18	- **Real customer data, new tools and break-glass need a request.** Each has a named approver and a time limit.
19	    19	
20	    20	## 1. Daily development (non-prod)
21	    21	
22	    22	- **What you do:** use Claude Code as you do today, with non-prod roles. Manual permission mode is the
23	    23	  default; you may switch to auto mode (D1). Commands that run inside the sandbox run without a prompt
24	    24	  (phase 2, OD12).
25	    25	- **Approval:** none (risk level L1).
26	    26	- **What is different:** the organisation's managed settings apply to everyone; bypass mode is
27	    27	  removed; plugins and MCP servers come from the catalogue only (section 6). From phase 2 the sandbox
28	    28	  hides credentials and blocks Unix sockets, so `git push`, `gh`, Docker and private-registry `npm ci` fail inside it: run
29	    29	  them yourself at the `!` prompt. Using `--restricted` is recommended (D3).
30	    30	- **Workarounds (OD34):** ask the agent to write the PR text to a file, then run `git push` and
31	    31	  `gh pr create --body-file <file>` at the `!` prompt; run Docker-based tests in CI on the PR;
32	    32	  private packages install with the read-only registry token set up for you. For prod questions use
33	    33	  metrics and masked logs through `ProdReadMetadata` (section 4) before asking for real data (section 5).
34	    34	- **From phase 1** each `aws`, `pulumi` or `serverless` call asks you first, in auto mode too
35	    35	  (OD43): until standing prod write is removed, your sign-in can still change prod.
36	    36	- **From phase 2 you will also notice** (layer 2, examples E8): each WebFetch asks; your own and the project's permission
37	    37	  rules are ignored, so prompts may rise; sign-in is locked to Papaya's organisation (API-key sessions
38	    38	  are refused) and the minimum Claude Code version rises; on macOS, servers on localhost fail inside
39	    39	  the sandbox; native Windows is not supported (use WSL2).
40	    40	- **Layer:** [2](01-framework.md#layer-2--agent-runtime-controls).
41	    41	
42	    42	## 2. Reading prod
43	    43	
44	    44	- **What you do:** with `ProdReadMetadata` (1-hour session) you and your agent read metrics, metadata
45	    45	  and logs that are redacted at source and masked by a data protection policy (OD28): identifiers
46	    46	  such as national IDs, bank accounts and diagnoses show as masked values. Lambda configuration is readable per service once its secrets
47	    47	  are resolved at runtime; until then, read timeout and memory from the IaC code.
48	    48	- **Approval:** none (L0).
49	    49	- **Cost to know:** in the first months, raw logs of services not yet redacted are not readable
50	    50	  without a data-read request (section 5). This is the largest cost of the transition.
51	    51	- **Remember:** the agent uses **your** AWS SSO session, so it can do whatever you can (layer 1). Keep
52	    52	  the portal session short.
53	    53	- **Layer:** [1](01-framework.md#layer-1--identity-and-access).
54	    54	
55	    55	## 3. Shipping a prod change
56	    56	
57	    57	1. Write the change as code (Pulumi, `serverless.yml`, Kubernetes manifests) and preview it on non-prod.
58	    58	2. Push the branch and open a pull request. The PR runs secret scanning, dependency checks and SAST
59	    59	   (S10), and previews non-prod only.
60	    60	3. One code owner of the changed files approves. You cannot approve your own PR, and the approver may
61	    61	   not be the last person who pushed. An agent never approves a PR (OD5). Managed settings deny `gh pr review` for agents, but
62	    62	   that is hygiene only: another form of the same call gets past it, so the approval-gate check
63	    63	   flags approvals that look automated rather than blocking them (OD25).
64	    64	   - Domain code and stacks: your domain team. Members of the on-call group are co-owners, but
65	    65	     their approval counts for another team's files only on an incident PR while they are on shift;
66	    66	     the approval-gate check enforces it (OD27). A PR that touches several teams' files needs an
67	    67	     owner of each.
68	    68	   - Process files (`.github/`, `CLAUDE.md`, `.claude/`, the catalogue, the SCP and IAM stacks,
69	    69	     `tools/risk-stop/`, `tools/ci/`, `oncall/`): **two** members of the L3 owner team (OD26,
70	    70	     OD32). A night fix that needs an IAM change goes through JIT.
71	    71	   - Clicking "Update branch" after someone else's merge keeps your approvals as long as your own
72	    72	     changes are the same; a push that changes them needs a new approval (OD31).
73	    73	4. Merge (squash only). The deploy job previews prod and applies the change.
74	    74	5. **If the deploy stops at the risk stop** (stateful replace or delete, IAM, network, a policy
75	    75	   finding): open a second PR that adds only `deploy-approvals/<stack>/<stopped commit>.yaml` with the
76	    76	   hash from the job summary. By default the first approver approves it; if they are unavailable,
77	    77	   another owner of the stack does, which is recorded as a deviation (OD13, OD11). Merging it deploys
78	    78	   if the new prod preview has the same hash. While the stack is stopped, later merges to it stop too.
79	    79	
80	    80	- **Time:** same working day from PR to prod; approval wait ≤ 1 hour in working hours (S4 targets).
81	    81	- **What CI does differently (OD22):** npm install scripts do not run in preview and deploy jobs;
82	    82	  if a package needs its script, ask the L3 owner team to add it to `tools/ci/allowed-install-scripts.txt`.
83	    83	  A stack may create IAM roles for its own services only as `svc-*` roles with the standard
84	    84	  permissions boundary; roles that read claim data (`app-claims-*`) are created in the IAM stack
85	    85	  and referenced by ARN. PRs that touch infrastructure code also get an automated agent review,
86	    86	  which is advice, not an approval.
87	    87	- **Layer:** [3](01-framework.md#layer-3--change-workflow-by-risk-level); diagram
88	    88	  [`01-change-workflow`](../diagrams/01-change-workflow.svg).
89	    89	
90	    90	- **Other platforms (OD36, OD40):** mobile releases and over-the-air updates go through the same PR;
91	    91	  the CI publishes to the `production` EAS channel, and nobody runs `eas update` against it from a
92	    92	  laptop (your Expo role cannot). GCP prod access for a person is a Privileged Access Manager
93	    93	  request approved by the on-call approver, never a standing role; k0s access for people is
94	    94	  read-only through single sign-on once OIDC is in place.
95	    95	
96	    96	## 3a. Database changes and data fixes
97	    97	
98	    98	- **Schema and metadata:** write the migration (or GraphQL-engine metadata change) as a file under
99	    99	  `db/<service>/`, open a PR, get your domain owner's approval as for code. After merge the `sql`
100	   100	  deploy job applies it with its own database role; nobody, you included, holds database
101	   101	  credentials (OD29, ADR-0011).
102	   102	- **Data fix** (a stuck claim, a payout to retry): a file `db/<service>/data-fixes/<tenant>/<ticket>.sql`
103	   103	  for one tenant, with a `-- expected_rows: N` header. It needs a code owner **and** a different
104	   104	  person from that tenant's data owners (L3-data-write). The job rolls it back if the row count
105	   105	  differs, and its summary shows counts only. Name records by their internal IDs only: no account
106	   106	  numbers, national IDs, names or diagnoses in the file. If the fix needs such a value, the data
107	   107	  owner uploads it as a values file and your SQL uses `:'variable'`; the `data-fix-scan` check fails
108	   108	  the PR otherwise (OD48).
109	   109	- **Expect a stop** for `DROP`, `TRUNCATE`, column type changes, `DELETE`/`UPDATE` without a
110	   110	  `WHERE`, grants and row-level security, and every metadata change: open the
111	   111	  `deploy-approvals/` PR as in step 5 above. Prefer expand/contract migrations.
112	   112	- **In an incident:** the same path; the on-call approver may stand in for the data owner, who
113	   113	  reviews it the next working day.
114	   114	- **Layer:** [3](01-framework.md#layer-3--change-workflow-by-risk-level).
115	   115	
116	   116	## 4. An incident at 2 a.m.
117	   117	
118	   118	You are the **incident responder**. The **on-call approver** only approves; they never write the fix (OD7).
119	   119	
120	   120	1. Start an incident-analysis session with read-only roles, in an empty scratch directory outside
121	   121	   the repository: `claude --restricted --strict-mcp-config --tools "Bash,Read,Grep,Glob"` (no
122	   122	   WebFetch, no MCP servers; Bash can still reach the network). Read metrics and masked logs; the
123	   123	   `incident-triage` skill guides the session.
124	   124	2. Open (or find) the incident issue in Linear. Make the fix in a normal session, preview on
125	   125	   non-prod, and open a PR labelled `incident` that links the issue: the on-call approval counts
126	   126	   only while the issue is open and the approver is on shift (OD27).
127	   127	3. Call the on-call approver (phone in phase 1; routed alerts from phase 2). They review and approve.
128	   128	   If they find a problem, you push the fix and they approve again.
129	   129	4. Merge; the deploy job applies the change. If it stops at the risk stop, the approval PR it
130	   130	   needs (`deploy-approvals/<stack>/`) goes the same way: label it `incident` and link the same
131	   131	   open issue, or the approval-gate check does not count the on-call approval on it either.
132	   132	
133	   133	- **Time:** target ≤ 15 min waiting for approval (S7); 11–46 min from decision to apply is an
134	   134	  estimate (⚠️), measured first during rollout against a 30-minute target.
135	   135	- **Blockers to know:** a risky change already waiting on `main` blocks your fix for that stack until
136	   136	  it is approved or reverted; at night, process files (workflows, `CLAUDE.md`, catalogue) wait for the
137	   137	  L3 owner team, or the JIT fallback applies.
138	   138	- **Only if the PR path cannot be used** (GitHub Actions down, broken pipeline, an operation not in
139	   139	  IaC): end your AWS portal session and sign in fresh, then open a JIT request issue in Linear from
140	   140	  its template (outside GitHub), with the exact commands; it is the record of the request (OD30). The on-call approver approves before the grant by
141	   141	  moving the issue to "Approved"; the grant then arrives automatically, and is refused if you
142	   142	  approved it yourself, the approver is not on shift or the incident is closed (OD33).
143	   143	  You get `InfraOperator-<service>` (1-hour role session; the real window can approach 2 h) and type
144	   144	  the commands yourself, in a terminal **without an agent**. Afterwards your commands are compared
145	   145	  with CloudTrail (by hand in phase 1, by a job from phase 2), and you open a PR that codifies the change.
146	   146	- **Layers:** [3](01-framework.md#layer-3--change-workflow-by-risk-level),
147	   147	  [7](01-framework.md#layer-7--observability-audit-incident-response-and-break-glass); diagram
148	   148	  [`03-incident-lane`](../diagrams/03-incident-lane.svg).
149	   149	
150	   150	## 5. Reading real customer data
151	   151	
152	   152	- **What you do:** end your AWS portal session and sign in fresh, then open a data-read request issue
153	   153	  in Linear from its template, with one tenant, purpose, store, time window and the agreement that
154	   154	  covers it (OD30). You get a data-read role for 1 hour.
155	   155	  After reading one tenant's data, do not post to shared places without review.
156	   156	- **Approval:** an approver who is not you, plus the data owner. At night the on-call approver
157	   157	  approves alone, and the data owner reviews it the next working day.
158	   158	- **PHI (medical records):** you read it yourself, in a terminal **without an agent**; give the agent
159	   159	  only a redacted summary. A store that holds PHI counts as PHI unless the agent reads a view without
160	   160	  it. Partner-uploaded claim documents never go into an agent session raw: reproduce with synthetic
161	   161	  documents, or de-identify them first.
162	   162	- **Non-prod** should hold no real data; a store not yet scanned follows this section's rule.
163	   163	- **Layer:** [6](01-framework.md#layer-6--data-protection-and-prompt-injection-defence).
164	   164	
165	   165	## 6. Adding a plugin or MCP server
166	   166	
167	   167	- **What you do:** open a request with what the tool reads, where it sends data and which write
168	   168	  tools it needs. A local MCP server is admitted only as a container image pinned by digest or as
169	   169	  code inside a pinned plugin, not as `npx -y <package>` (OD26). Keep your GitHub CLI token in the
170	   170	  system credential store (`gh auth status` shows where it is). A catalogue entry is added by a PR with a review record (examples
171	   171	  [`reviews/`](../examples/claude/marketplace/reviews/)).
172	   172	- **Approval:** two members of the L3 owner team (the catalogue is a process path, OD26).
173	   173	- **Time:** decided within 5 working days (S6).
174	   174	- **Not allowed:** installing a plugin or MCP server outside the catalogue, or sideloading one with
175	   175	  command-line flags.
176	   176	- **Layer:** [4](01-framework.md#layer-4--supply-chain-for-mcp-servers-and-plugins).
177	   177	
178	   178	## 7. When you are the on-call approver
179	   179	
180	   180	- You are on a named 24/7 schedule: a primary and a backup. The primary approves; the backup steps in
181	   181	  only if the primary is unavailable (OD2).
182	   182	- While on call you **only approve**: you do not write fixes or request JIT grants (OD7). A night
183	   183	  incident therefore needs two people awake: the responder and you.
184	   184	- Target: approve within 15 minutes (S7). Approve JIT only when the PR path cannot be used, and record
185	   185	  why you refuse it otherwise.
186	   186	- Approve another domain's PR only if it is labelled `incident`, links an open incident, and you
187	   187	  are on shift (OD9, OD27); the approval-gate check does not count it otherwise.
188	   188	- **Layers:** [3](01-framework.md#layer-3--change-workflow-by-risk-level),
189	   189	  [7](01-framework.md#layer-7--observability-audit-incident-response-and-break-glass).
190	   190	
191	   191	## 8. Shared agent knowledge
192	   192	
193	   193	`CLAUDE.md` and other agent configuration files define how the whole team works, so changes to them
194	   194	are approved by two members of the L3 owner team; a domain-team approval does not count (OD3, OD26). Review your agent's auto memory
195	   195	and delete it after a suspicious session (D3). The shared `CLAUDE.md` starts from the template in
196	   196	`examples/claude/repo-templates/CLAUDE.md`; pull requests use the template in
197	   197	`examples/github/pull_request_template.md`, which asks which parts an agent wrote.
198	   198	
199	   199	## 9. Using the agent for DevSecOps tasks
200	   200	
201	   201	The internal plugin `devsecops-guardrails` carries the skills; invoke them by describing the task
202	   202	([framework §2](01-framework.md#2-agent-assisted-devsecops-workflows)):
203	   203	
204	   204	| Task | Skill | Where you run it | What you get |
205	   205	|---|---|---|---|
206	   206	| Ship an infrastructure change | `prod-change` | normal session | IaC change, non-prod preview, PR text |
207	   207	| Triage an alert | `incident-triage` | incident-analysis session (section 4) | likely cause, smallest fix, JIT command list if needed |
208	   208	| Understand a stopped deploy before approving | `risk-summary-explainer` | normal session, or the CI agent's comment | what each stopped operation does and whether it can be undone |
209	   209	| Fix a vulnerable dependency | `dependency-fix` | normal session, or a CI-agent PR | one small PR per advisory |
210	   210	
211	   211	The agent drafts; you approve nothing it wrote yourself, and nobody approves through an agent.
212	   212	
213	   213	## Where the evidence comes from
214	   214	
215	   215	You do not write separate evidence: the PR, its approvals, the deploy run and CloudTrail form the
216	   216	record of every prod change. Compliance's view is in
217	   217	[`04-compliance-mapping.md`](04-compliance-mapping.md).
218	   218	# Rollout plan: 45 / 75 / 100 days
219	   219	
220	   220	> Status: moved out of framework layer 8 on 2026-11-09 and expanded. The items, their order and the
221	   221	> phase-1 subset were approved with the framework (OD4, OD7, OD21); the allowlist became two repo
222	   222	> scripts after examples finding 19. Added here and approved by the author (owner of this submission, not Papaya) on
223	   223	> 2026-11-09 ("done when" checks stay [design]): the owner and "done when" of each item, the "measured from" column, item 2.9 (from OD15,
224	   224	> OD20), the run-log export in 2.4 (from layer 3, G7) and the S4 risk (framing §5). After the
225	   225	> independent review, the owner approved fixes that add or change items (from OD22: 1.6, 1.12, 1.15, 1.17,
226	   226	> 1.18, 1.19–1.23, 1.11, 2.2, 2.4, 2.9, 2.10; from OD31: 1.6, 1.8, 1.11, 1.13, 1.16, 2.8, 2.11–2.13,
227	   227	> S4 and the effort estimate) · Updated:
228	   228	> 2026-11-09 · Builds on [`01-framework.md`](01-framework.md)
229	   229	
230	   230	## How to read this
231	   231	
232	   232	The rollout takes about 100 days (re-baselined from the 90 of GĐ-12 after the effort estimate, OD49). Effort is estimated roughly in
233	   233	[Load and risks](#load-and-risks) (⚠️ no Papaya data): the 23 phase-1 items do not fit 30 days with

    87	## Evidence for one prod change (S8)
    88	
    89	**Target** (framing §5): for a prod change picked at random, show who proposed, who approved, what
    90	was approved, what was applied and when, in ≤ 30 minutes, without asking anyone. Not yet timed
    91	(⚠️; first measured in rollout).
    92	
    93	Start **backward**, from a prod write in CloudTrail: unlike starting from a PR, this also finds
    94	unapproved writes, as the monthly reconciliation does (S3).
    95	
    96	| Step | Question | Record | Where |
    97	|---|---|---|---|
    98	| 1 | What was applied, when? | Write event: `eventTime`, `eventName`, resource; session name `deploy-<run_id>-<attempt>` [design, E3] in `principalId` (📖 R2.5.3) | CloudTrail; digests prove integrity (📖 R2.6.4) |
    99	| 2 | Which run, which commits? | Run ID → deploy run: stack, commit SHA, preview, risk-stop result. A run can deploy several commits: GitHub cancels a pending run when a newer one arrives, so the run deploys every commit on `main` between the stack's previous successful deploy and its own SHA ([examples, limits of the risk stop](../examples/README.md#limits-of-the-risk-stop)) | Actions log (⚠️ G7; export Ph 2) |
   100	| 3 | What was approved? | Each of those commits → its squash-merged PR (OD16). Stale approvals are dismissed (📖 R3.2.3), so approval covers the final diff | GitHub PR |
   101	| 4 | Who proposed? | PR author; for an app-opened PR, the person who triggered it, from the approval-gate check (G19) | GitHub PR |
   102	| 5 | Who approved, before apply? | Review name and time; approver ≠ author, ≠ last pusher (📖 R3.2.3, R3.3.1); approver owns the path (CODEOWNERS at that commit). Approval < merge < `eventTime` | GitHub PR; git |
   103	| 6 | Was the gate on? | E1 copy; no `repository_ruleset.update` or `protected_branch.policy_override` between the approval and `eventTime`; G8 results | git; audit-log export |
   104	| 7 | Did the risk stop fire? | `risk-summary`; `deploy-approvals/` PR with hash and stack-owner approval; second run shows the hash matched | artifact (⚠️ G7); git; PR |
   105	
   106	From Ph 2 the change record (C-19) holds these links, so steps 2–7 are one lookup. In Ph 1 there is
   107	no change record or reconciliation, but the nightly export (OD30) keeps every record in the evidence
   108	bucket, so nothing expires (Actions logs 90 days by default, 📖 R9.1.8; audit log 180 days, 📖 R3.5.6);
   109	the auditor follows the links by hand. S8 ≤ 30 min is realistic from Ph 2 (⚠️ inference).
   110	
   111	**Serverless stacks:** CloudFormation makes the changes with the stack's `deploymentRole` (layer 3),
   112	so those events may not carry the run's session name (⚠️ not researched). The link is the deploy
   113	session's CloudFormation call plus the stack's events.
   114	
   115	**Incident lane:** the same chain, plus the `incident` label and the on-call schedule showing the
   116	approver was the primary on shift, or the backup while the primary was unavailable (O-7). The wait
   117	(S7) runs from review request to approval. In Ph 1 the approver is called by phone, so paging time is
   118	not recorded (G5).
   119	
   120	**JIT fallback**, keyed by the JIT request ID ([layer 7](01-framework.md#layer-7--observability-audit-incident-response-and-break-glass)):
   121	(1) proposed: command list, scope, reason, incident link, in a Linear request issue (independent of GitHub; mirrored to the evidence bucket, OD30);
   122	(2) approved: on-call approver ≠ requester, before the grant, checked by the JIT receiver before it calls `CreateAccountAssignment` (OD33, E16); (3) granted: `CreateAccountAssignment`
   123	and `DeleteAccountAssignment` (📖 R2.4.2); (4) applied: CloudTrail writes of the
   124	`InfraOperator-<service>` session, the human named by `onBehalfOf.userId` where present (📖 R2.5.1),
   125	else by session name and directory lookup, not a stable key (⚠️ R2.5.3); (5) reconciled: writes compared with the list, codify PR merged, drift
   126	ticket until then. The approver approved a **command list**, not the applied change; a write outside
   127	the list is found afterwards, not prevented.

31	## A. Limits and trade-offs, in detail
32	
33	- **The fallback meets the approval rule only partly** (approves a command list, not an applied
34	  change); accepted by the author (Options §9 Q2), to be signed off by Papaya's Compliance (§1). It is a second, process-controlled path, while the
35	  framing asked for one technically enforced path (framing §3.3, Options §7). It stays narrow only
36	  if most incidents are expressible in IaC (unknown, Options §8); layer 7 measures this.
37	- **On GitHub Team nobody sees the prod diff before apply** (⚠️ R4.6 #1; Team assumed, GĐ-5).
38	  Risky prod diffs stop the deploy until an owner of the stack approves the prod preview [design].
39	- **Admins can edit the gate**; logged, not prevented (logging 📖 R3.2.2; ability to edit ⚠️ R3.2.2,
40	  R3.6 #1). An admin's agent has
41	  the same power, because the agent uses its engineer's GitHub login (⚠️ R6.5 #10).
42	- **Some rules are process, not technology:** see "Process rules" in layer 1. The owner's rule
43	  "the PR approver is always an engineer, never an agent" (OD5) is absolute as policy, but on
44	  laptops it rests on policy, training and managed deny rules for `gh pr review` (OD25), which
45	  are hygiene: another form of the same call is not matched (📖 R9.4.1). An agent could still
46	  approve through its engineer's login. A review does not show whether it came from the web or
47	  the API (📖 R9.1.10); the approval-gate app only flags suspicious approvals (OD27). And "named"
48	  means a GitHub account that a register maps to a person: SAML SSO needs Enterprise Cloud
49	  (📖 R9.1.2), so on Team the mapping is a process (layer 1, OD25).
50	- **Incident approvers vs domain review:** code-owner review means an approver must own the file,
51	  at L2 as at L3. So that one on-call primary can approve any deployable path at 2 a.m., the on-call approver
52	  group co-owns every deployable path (owner decision OD9, layer 3). GitHub accepts an
53	  approval from any listed owner (📖 R3.2.7), so the approval-gate app enforces the rest (OD27,
54	  [design]): an on-call approval counts for another team's file only if the PR links an open
55	  incident and the approver is on shift. A label alone grants nothing, since anyone with Triage
56	  can apply it (📖 R9.1.9). Because on-call approvers only
57	  approve (OD7), a night incident needs two people awake: the incident responder and the on-call
58	  approver (the backup only replaces an unavailable primary).
59	- **One approver for most high-risk changes.** L3 changes in deployable code (IAM, stateful
60	  deletes, network) get one approver, like L2, from the owners of the path (the stack's owners for
61	  L3 content in domain files, OD8), and risky prod diffs stop for a look at the prod preview (OD2,
62	  OD8, layer 3). A single reviewer can miss things; this is the owner's trade-off for speed. The
63	  exception is the **process paths** (workflows, CODEOWNERS, agent config, catalogue, SCP and IAM
64	  stacks, risk stop): two L3 owner team members, enforced by the approval-gate app (OD26). They change
65	  rarely, are never urgent at night, and one compromised login must not be enough to change them.
66	- **k0s and Firebase are weaker:** no prod preview or risk stop, no break-glass when Actions is
67	  down (G1, G2), and their deploy credentials are stored in GitHub (OD1). For k0s, the interim
68	  controls of OD24 (a namespaced, time-limited deploy token and the Kubernetes API audit log) rely
69	  on `extraArgs`, which is "outside k0s support" (📖 R9.3.1).
70	- **New dependencies on two GitHub Apps** (required check, CI agent): if the required-check app is
71	  down, every merge to `main` is blocked, incident PRs included; that counts as "pipeline
72	  unavailable" for JIT. The required-check app now enforces OD26 and OD27 too, so it is a hard
73	  phase-1 prerequisite (rollout); its decision logic is an example (E12), its keys and hosting are
74	  open (G19). It is also the longest phase-1 item (10–15 person-days, ⚠️ estimate, OD35).
75	- **HIPAA applicability is a legal question** (⚠️ R1.11.1.11); the design treats Papaya as a
76	  business associate, as the brief implies.

81	
82	- **SCPs on the prod OU** [design] (SCPs cap member-account principals, 📖 R2.3.1, R2.3.2):
83	  - deny data-plane reads on claim stores except application roles and the approved data-read role,
84	    by `aws:PrincipalArn` (📖 R2.3.8; pattern ⚠️ R2.9 #4). Actions, e.g. `s3:GetObject`,
85	    `sqs:ReceiveMessage`, `states:GetExecutionHistory`, are incomplete and unchecked (⚠️ G13);
86	  - deny `lambda:UpdateFunctionCode` / `lambda:UpdateFunctionConfiguration` (⚠️ R4.6 #3) except
87	    CloudFormation `deploymentRole`s, the Pulumi prod deploy role (if Pulumi manages Lambdas) and the
88	    JIT roles. The Serverless prod deploy role is a separate role and is not exempt: it only passes
89	    the `deploymentRole` (examples finding 13). This closes `serverless deploy function`, which changes config outside CloudFormation
90	    (📖 R4.4.4), and needs `deploymentRole` set on every Serverless stack (key 📖 R4.4.5; need ⚠️ R4.6 #3);
91	  - a pre-deployed revocation Deny on `identitystore:UserId` (📖 R2.4.4); deny changes to any trail
92	    in prod accounts, since member accounts cannot touch the organization trail anyway (📖 R2.6.2;
93	    examples findings 10, 15);
94	  - exempt role names are protected: only the IAM stack's deploy role may create or change such
95	    roles (OD19), and from phase 1 that is a role of its own (OD22): the IAM stack deploys from a
96	    separate GitHub environment, `production-iam`, whose OIDC subject only that role trusts. So
97	    code running in a domain stack's deploy job cannot obtain it. Domain deploy roles (and the
98	    CloudFormation `deploymentRole` of each Serverless stack) may create or change only `svc-*`
99	    roles, and only with a fixed permissions boundary attached that they cannot remove or edit
100	    (pattern 📖 R9.2.1; role action list ⚠️; examples E4b). The boundary denies `iam:*` and
101	    root sessions. Cost: Lambda and ECS roles that read claim data (`app-claims-*`) live in the
102	    IAM stack and are referenced by ARN (examples finding 16);
103	  - deny every action of `OrganizationAccountAccessRole` in the prod OU (OD23). Organizations
104	    creates this role with "full administrative permissions" in each account it creates, trusted
105	    by the management account (📖 R9.2.4); SCPs cover it as any other member-account role
106	    (📖 R9.2.6, inference). Using it in an emergency needs an SCP change, an L3 path.
107	  - Limits: 10 SCPs per target, 10,240 characters; no SCP applies to the management account
108	    (📖 R2.3.2, R2.3.4), so whatever deploys SCPs there is the most sensitive role (L3 path, held by the L3 owner team only, not co-owned by the on-call group; OD13).

113	
114	- **Who administers the administrators (OD23).** Whoever administers IAM Identity Center can
115	  assign themselves any permission set, so "no standing prod write" holds only if that power is
116	  itself controlled [design unless marked]:
117	  - permission sets and account assignments are code in an identity stack (an L3 path, L3 owner

123	    which account's trail records changes made from a delegated administrator is not documented

129	    detective control only;
130	  - member-account root users: credentials removed through centralized root access; privileged

136	
137	- **CI → GCP (OD36):** Workload Identity Federation. Google requires a condition that limits the pool
138	  to Papaya's GitHub organization and advises the numeric `*_id` claims, which cannot be reused (📖
139	  [WIF with deployment pipelines](https://docs.cloud.google.com/iam/docs/workload-identity-federation-with-deployment-pipelines);
140	  R3.4.5b). Narrower than that, as on AWS [design]: the pool condition also names the monorepo by
141	  `repository_id`; `google.subject` maps `assertion.sub` (📖 same page), so the subject carries the
142	  environment (`repo:…:environment:production`, 📖 R3.4.3); and only the `production` subject may
143	  impersonate the prod service account. Granting by subject rather than by a mapped attribute is
144	  ⚠️ (the page shows the `principalSet …/attribute.` form, which works with an `environment`
145	  attribute mapped from the token: also ⚠️, since the page lists no GitHub `environment` claim).
146	  Vertex AI model and endpoint changes deploy this way, from the monorepo, like any other stack.
147	- **GCP for humans and agents (OD36) [design unless marked]:** no standing role on prod projects for
148	  people. Agents and engineers get a custom read-metadata role (no `storage.objects.get`, no Vertex
149	  prediction calls such as `generateContent`, which is a data read, 📖 R9.6.3); writes and data reads
150	  come from Privileged Access Manager entitlements with approval, time-bound (30 min to 7 days, 📖
151	  R9.6.1), approved by the on-call approver. Whether PAM stops a requester approving their own
152	  grant is not documented (📖 R9.6.1 "not found"), so the entitlement lists the on-call group as

155	  that hold partner documents; cost: log volume. The HIPAA list names the renamed products

186	## E. AWS credentials on laptops
187	
188	- **Trade-off on AWS credentials [design].** With `~/.aws` hidden from the sandbox, phase 2 lists
189	  `aws *`, `pulumi *` and `serverless *` in `sandbox.excludedCommands`. Excluded commands run "with
190	  full access" (📖 R1.6.4), network included ("no filesystem restrictions and no network proxy", 📖 [sandboxing](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sandboxing.md#run-commands-outside-the-sandbox-with-excludedcommands)). Matching follows `Bash(...)` rule
191	  syntax on the command text (same page; details in examples finding 22); each excluded
192	  call prompts through the `ask` rules of layer 2. This is worse than an
193	  egress channel: `pulumi preview` runs the Pulumi program and `serverless` loads its config and
194	  plugins, all code in the repo that the agent can edit, so excluding them lets repo code run
195	  outside the sandbox with network access and with `~/.aws` readable (⚠️ inference). For these
196	  commands the sandbox gives no protection. And an injected `aws` command could send out the SSO
197	  token cache itself. That token likely opens every role assigned to the engineer for the rest of the
198	  portal session (📖 R2.1.5; token reuse ⚠️ R2.2.2), probably including JIT or data-read grants added
199	  later in that session (⚠️ inference). Mitigations [design]: a short portal session (📖 R2.1.5); end
200	  the existing portal session and sign in fresh **before** a JIT or data-read grant is created
201	  (whether ending a session invalidates a token already stolen is unverified ⚠️; ending it does not
202	  end role sessions, 📖 R2.4.3); an SCP that denies writes to resources outside Papaya's organization using
203	  `aws:ResourceOrgID` (key 📖 R2.3.8), on every OU, since the token can be stolen from a non-prod
204	  session; legitimate writes to outside resources need exceptions (⚠️ not inventoried). That SCP only stops Papaya's own credentials writing to a
205	  foreign bucket; it does not stop a command that sends the token to a non-AWS endpoint or uses the
206	  attacker's credentials (⚠️ inference). Prefer running `pulumi` and `serverless` against real
207	  accounts only in CI; on laptops keep them to non-prod roles, and move them into the phase-3
208	  container. Residual risk: token theft during a session. It is accepted
209	  because the engineer holds no **standing** prod write and no **standing** PHI read; during a JIT
210	  or data-read window the protection is the process rule in layer 1 (D2). Stronger option, phase 3:
211	  a separate OS user or container for prod-reading sessions
212	  (⚠️ R6.5 #2).

24	    24	| [0012](0012-approval-integrity-checked-by-the-gate-app.md) | The approval-gate app checks approval integrity: two approvals on process paths, on-call approvals only for open incidents | 3, 4 |
25	    25	
26	    26	Not recorded as ADRs, because they follow from the decisions above: the audit chain (change records,
27	    27	monthly reconciliation, drift detection; framework layer 7), the rollout plan
28	    28	([`../03-rollout-plan.md`](../03-rollout-plan.md)) and the CI-agent setup
29	    29	(layer 5; covered in parts by ADR-0006 and ADR-0007).
30	    30	
31	    31	Rule: an accepted ADR is not edited. A changed decision gets a new ADR that supersedes the old one.
32	    32	
33	    33	## Refinements since acceptance
34	    34	
35	    35	Writing and testing the files in [`../../examples/`](../../examples/README.md) made some details more
36	    36	precise. None changes a decision, so no ADR is superseded; the framework carries the current wording.
37	    37	
38	    38	- **ADR-0003:** "merge approval = deploy approval" gains two conditions: squash-only merges (OD16)
39	    39	  and deploying only the current tip of `main`, because a writer can re-run an old deploy run for
40	    40	  30 days and roll prod back without approval (OD17; examples finding 4).
41	    41	- **ADR-0004:** "the approver sees the prod diff" means the approver sees **which** prod resources and
42	    42	  properties change, not the new values, which stay out of the job summary so that secrets stay out of
43	    43	  logs; values are reviewed in the code of the stopped PR. The approval is also bound to git history
44	    44	  (examples E7, finding 2), and an early approval can match a later change outside the stack, an
45	    45	  accepted gap until G19 (OD18).
46	    46	- **ADR-0007:** the "read-only allowlist" became two exact repo scripts, because Claude Code already runs
47	    47	  read-only commands without a prompt and wildcard rules can write files (examples finding 19); phase 1
48	    48	  adds a `Read(~/.aws/**)` deny rule and `autoMode.classifyAllShell` (OD21). `sandbox.excludedCommands`
49	    49	  entries need a trailing ` *` and are paired with `ask` rules, so each excluded CLI call prompts, auto
50	    50	  mode included (examples finding 22).
51	    51	
52	    52	After the independent review (`work/07-review.md`; owner decisions from OD22, 2026-11-09). Two
53	    53	changes are decisions and got their own ADR: ADR-0011 (database changes) and ADR-0012, which
54	    54	supersedes parts of ADR-0003 and ADR-0010. The others narrow how a decision is carried out:
55	    55	
56	    56	- **ADR-0002:** "nobody holds standing prod write" now also covers who administers Identity Center:
57	    57	  permission sets and assignments are code owned by the L3 owner team only, other changes raise an
58	    58	  alert, `OrganizationAccountAccessRole` is denied in the prod OU and member-account root
59	    59	  credentials are removed (OD23). The management account stays outside SCPs: detected, not prevented.
60	    60	- **ADR-0003 / ADR-0004:** what runs in the deploy job is limited from phase 1: one GitHub
61	    61	  environment per kind of stack (`production-iam` for the IAM stack), bounded domain deploy roles,
62	    62	  no install scripts except a reviewed allowlist, and an agent review on infrastructure PRs (OD22).
63	    63	  This was OD20's phase-2 roadmap item. The risk stop's scope is unchanged (OD15).
64	    64	- **ADR-0008:** the k0s exception gets conditions: a separate `production-k0s` environment (was
65	    65	  optional), a namespaced, time-limited ServiceAccount token instead of a kubeconfig, and the

67	    67	- **ADR-0006:** its example entry `serverCommand` = `["npx", "<package>@<exact-version>"]` is no longer allowed: it pins the package, not its dependencies. "Pinned catalogue" now covers what reaches every laptop: the marketplace is pinned
68	    68	  to a protected release tag, every plugin (internal ones too) to a commit, auto-update is off, and
69	    69	  local MCP servers are admitted only as immutable artifacts (OD26).
70	    70	- **ADR-0003 / ADR-0007:** managed deny rules for `gh pr review` and the `gh` token file from phase 1,
71	    71	  as hygiene behind OD5; a login register maps GitHub accounts to people (OD25). The parts of

73	    73	- **ADR-0004:** the SQL risk stop of ADR-0011 adds stops for DML in migrations and for every

89	=== docs/adr/0001-prod-changes-only-through-ci.md
90	     1	# ADR-0001: Every production change goes through a reviewed PR applied by CI
91	     2	
92	     3	- **Status:** Accepted
93	     4	- **Date:** 2026-11-09
94	     5	- **Decided by:** owner of this submission (Options §9, "A + D2'")
95	     6	- **Scope:** all writes to production AWS, GCP, k0s and Firebase; incidents included (k0s and Firebase
96	     7	  have no risk stop and no break-glass yet, G1, G2; human GCP access is open, G3)
97	     8	
98	     9	## 1. Context
99	    10	
100	    11	Engineering wants Claude Code to talk to AWS directly; Compliance wants no production change without
101	    12	a named human who reviewed and approved it. "Most engineers' profiles can reach production" (brief), and deploys from laptops are assumed
102	    13	(GĐ-10, unconfirmed), so an agent on that laptop can deploy too. Incidents are where the pressure to bypass
103	    14	review is highest.
104	    15	
105	    16	## 2. Options considered
106	    17	
107	    18	| Option | Pros | Cons |
108	    19	|---|---|---|
109	    20	| A. PR → approval → CI deploy for everything ("IaC first") | One path, approval before apply, evidence by construction | Slower incidents (est. 11–46 min ⚠️ vs 2–20 min, Options §6) |
110	    21	| B. SSM Automation runbooks with an approval step | Approval inside AWS | Not verified that it meets the approval rule (G6); only for operations someone scripted. Kept on the roadmap, verified in phase 2 (OD4) |
111	    22	| C. JIT direct access for the engineer + agent | Fastest | Approves access, not the change; agent holds prod write |
112	    23	| D. Hosted agent with its own identity | Clean separation | New platform; does not remove the need for approval |
113	    24	
114	    25	## 3. Decision
115	    26	
116	    27	"A + D2'": option A is the default path for every production change, incidents included. A narrow JIT
117	    28	fallback exists only when the PR path cannot be used during an incident (ADR-0005). The owner accepts
118	    29	that this fallback meets the approval rule only partly (Options §9 Q2). Incident target: ≤ 30 min from
119	    30	decision to apply.
120	    31	
121	    32	## 4. Consequences
122	    33	
123	    34	- **Positive:** the PR, its approvals, the run log and CloudTrail form one evidence chain keyed by
124	    35	  commit SHA. Agent-written and human-written changes pass the same checks (S10).
125	    36	- **Negative / trade-offs:** slower incident fixes; operations that are not in IaC must first be
126	    37	  written as code or a runbook. Two write paths remain (PR and JIT), while the framing asked for one.
127	    38	- **Risks & how we watch them:** the fallback stays narrow only if most incidents are expressible in
128	    39	  IaC (unknown, Options §8). Metrics: JIT grants per month, share of incidents needing non-IaC
129	    40	  operations; above about 25 % (⚠️ starting threshold), make the PR lane faster or add a runbook, never widen JIT.
130	    41	- **Example:** Lambda timeouts at 2 a.m. The responder's agent proposes `timeout` 30 → 90 s in
131	    42	  `serverless.yml`; the PR is labelled `incident`; the on-call approver reviews and approves; CI
132	    43	  packages, previews prod and deploys with the OIDC role. Estimate 11–46 min (⚠️ Options §6).
133	    44	- **Next steps:** measure the incident PR lane on one service first (phase 1).
134	    45	
135	    46	## 5. References
136	    47	
137	    48	- Framework §1 and layer 3; `work/03-options.md` §1, §6, §9.
138	    49	- Related: ADR-0002, ADR-0003, ADR-0005.
139	=== docs/adr/0002-no-standing-prod-write-read-only-agent-identity.md
140	     1	# ADR-0002: Nobody holds standing prod write; in prod, the engineer's (and so the agent's) only standing role reads metadata
141	     2	
142	     3	- **Status:** Accepted
143	     4	- **Date:** 2026-11-09
144	     5	- **Decided by:** owner of this submission (Options §9; D2)
145	     6	- **Scope:** AWS IAM Identity Center permission sets and SCPs on the prod OU; k0s, GCP and Firebase by the same principle
146	     7	
147	     8	## 1. Context
148	     9	
149	    10	On a laptop the agent uses the engineer's AWS SSO cache, and one portal session reaches every role
150	    11	assigned to that engineer (📖 R2.2.1, R2.2.2; token-reuse detail ⚠️ R2.2.2). A separate "agent"
151	    12	permission set therefore does not separate the agent from the engineer (⚠️ R2.9 #1). Whatever the
152	    13	engineer holds, the agent holds.
153	    14	
154	    15	## 2. Options considered
155	    16	
156	    17	| Option | Pros | Cons |
157	    18	|---|---|---|
158	    19	| A. Separate agent permission set, engineer keeps write | Looks like least privilege | Same SSO cache: the agent can still assume the write role |
159	    20	| B. No standing prod write for anyone; `ProdReadMetadata` as the only standing prod role | Agent cannot write prod with the engineer's identity | Engineers also lose direct writes and raw-log reads |
160	    21	| C. Separate OS user or container for agent sessions | Real separation of credentials | More setup; planned for phase 3 only |
161	    22	
162	    23	## 3. Decision
163	    24	
164	    25	Option B. Prod is written only by the CI pipeline role, or by an approved, time-boxed JIT grant
165	    26	(ADR-0005). The standing prod role is `ProdReadMetadata` [design name]: metrics, redacted log groups,
166	    27	configuration of services whose secrets are resolved at runtime; no data-plane reads of claim stores;
167	    28	1-hour role session, the minimum (📖 R2.1.4). From phase 2, SCPs on the prod OU deny data-plane reads and
168	    29	direct Lambda updates except for named roles (pattern ⚠️ R2.9 #4, R4.6 #3). Option C follows in phase 3.
169	    30	
170	    31	## 4. Consequences
171	    32	
172	    33	- **Positive:** once standing write and broad read roles are removed (end of phase 1), an agent,
173	    34	  even a manipulated one, cannot write prod AWS or read AWS claim stores with the engineer's standing
174	    35	  identity (data-plane action list ⚠️ G13); k0s and GCP follow the same principle, mechanisms open
175	    36	  (G1, G3). In non-prod the agent keeps broad rights (`NonProdDeveloper`, ADR-0010 L1). Compliance gets least privilege enforced by IAM (S1).
176	    37	- **Negative / trade-offs:** during the transition, engineers lose raw logs and configuration of
177	    38	  services not yet redacted. Configuration values then come from the IaC code; raw logs need a
178	    39	  data-read grant in an incident. Process rules remain where
179	    40	  IAM cannot separate engineer and agent: no agent in the JIT terminal (D2).
180	    41	- **Risks & how we watch them:** SSO-token theft during a session could open later grants (⚠️);
181	    42	  mitigations [design] are a short portal session and a fresh sign-in before a grant. The data-plane action
182	    43	  list is incomplete (⚠️ G13). Identity Center assignment export is reviewed quarterly.
183	    44	- **Next steps:** phase 1 removes broad read roles only after the minimal real-data read flow works,
184	    45	  then removes standing prod write once its prerequisites are in place.
185	    46	
186	    47	## 5. References
187	    48	
188	    49	- Framework layer 1, layer 2 ("Trade-off on AWS credentials"), layer 8 rollout.
189	    50	- Related: ADR-0001, ADR-0005, ADR-0009.
190	=== docs/adr/0003-merge-to-main-is-the-approval-gate.md
191	     1	# ADR-0003: The merge to `main` is the approval gate: two people, code owners, on-call co-ownership
192	     2	
193	     3	- **Status:** Accepted; superseded in part by [ADR-0012](0012-approval-integrity-checked-by-the-gate-app.md)
194	     4	  (which approvals count, two approvers on process paths, on-call approvals only in an incident)
195	     5	- **Date:** 2026-11-09
196	     6	- **Decided by:** owner of this submission (GĐ-5, GĐ-8, GĐ-11; OD2, OD5, OD7, OD9, OD10, OD13)
197	     7	- **Scope:** GitHub monorepo rulesets, CODEOWNERS, `production` environment, on-call schedule
198	     8	
199	     9	## 1. Context
200	    10	
201	    11	Papaya is assumed to be on GitHub Team (GĐ-5), where environment required reviewers do not exist for
202	    12	private repositories (📖 R3.1.2), so the approval must happen before the deploy job. Incidents need an
203	    13	approver within 15 minutes, 24/7 (S7), and code-owner review requires an approval from an owner of the files (📖 R3.2.3, R3.2.7;
204	    14	per-file behaviour ⚠️).
205	    15	
206	    16	## 2. Options considered
207	    17	
208	    18	| Option | Pros | Cons |
209	    19	|---|---|---|
210	    20	| A. Upgrade to Enterprise for environment reviewers | Approval sits next to the deploy | Cost; not assumed (GĐ-5) |
211	    21	| B. Merge to `main` as the gate; `production` limited to `main` | Works on Team; the approver sees the code that will be applied | Nobody sees the prod diff before apply (partly handled by ADR-0004) |
212	    22	| C. More approvers for high-risk changes | More eyes | Slower; the owner wants two people per change |
213	    23	
214	    24	## 3. Decision
215	    25	
216	    26	Option B. Ruleset on `main`: PR required, 1 approval, code-owner review, dismiss stale approvals,
217	    27	approval by someone other than the last pusher, required checks from a pinned source app, no force
218	    28	push, empty bypass list (📖 R3.2.2, R3.2.3, R3.2.5); branch up to date, since there is no merge queue
219	    29	(⚠️ R4.6 #1). `production` accepts only `main` (📖 R3.1.3).
220	    30	
221	    31	- **Merge = deploy approval** only if the reusable deploy workflow alone references `production`,
222	    32	  with no ref/SHA inputs, no `issue_comment`, `pull_request_target` or `workflow_run` triggers, one
223	    33	  concurrency group per stack without `cancel-in-progress` (📖 R4.1.4; ⚠️ R3.6 #1, from 📖 R3.1.3, R3.4.5c).
224	    34	- **Two people per change:** one makes it, one approves it; the approver is always an engineer,
225	    35	  never an agent (OD2, OD5). L3 changes need one approver too, who must own the path.
226	    36	- **Incidents:** on-call engineers only approve; an incident responder writes the fix (OD7).
227	    37	- **Night coverage:** an on-call approver group co-owns every deployable path in CODEOWNERS; one
228	    38	  primary, one backup (OD9). It does not co-own process-defining paths (`.github/**`, CODEOWNERS,
229	    39	  agent config, catalogue) or the SCP stack, which only the L3 owner team approves (OD13); IAM-only
230	    40	  stacks are deployable, so it co-owns them with the L3 owner team. *Superseded by OD32: the IAM
231	    41	  stack is a process path, L3 owner team only.*
232	    42	- **Agent review:** an independent agent may post an automated review; it never counts as an
233	    43	  approval (GĐ-11).
234	    44	- **Cross-team PRs:** one approval is enough (OD10). *Superseded by ADR-0012: each team's files need
235	    45	  their own owner's approval; the on-call approval covers another team's files only in an incident (OD27).*
236	    46	
237	    47	## 4. Consequences
238	    48	
239	    49	- **Positive:** four-eyes enforced by GitHub, not by the agent; one rule for normal days and incidents.
240	    50	- **Negative / trade-offs:** GitHub accepts an approval from any listed owner (📖 R3.2.7), so the
241	    51	  on-call group can approve another domain's PR; domain review on normal days is a process rule.
242	    52	- **Risks & how we watch them:** admins can edit the gate, logged, not prevented (⚠️ R3.2.2, R3.6 #1;
243	    53	  logging 📖 R3.2.2); alerts on ruleset changes; monthly report of cross-domain approvals. An agent could approve through its engineer's login; no detection found (⚠️). The
244	    54	  required-check app's hosting, key and triggers are open (⚠️ G19).
245	    55	- **Next steps:** rulesets, CODEOWNERS and its validation check in phase 1; the required-check app
246	    56	  before any agent workflow may open PRs; L3 owner team composition open (G17).
247	    57	
248	    58	## 5. References
249	    59	
250	    60	- Framework layer 3 ("Gate = merge to `main`", "Who approves at night"), layer 7 (audit alerts).
251	    61	- Related: ADR-0001, ADR-0004.
252	=== docs/adr/0004-risk-stop-on-risky-prod-diffs.md
253	     1	# ADR-0004: Risky prod diffs stop the deploy until a stack owner approves the prod preview
254	     2	
255	     3	- **Status:** Accepted; refined after the independent review (see [ADR index](README.md), "refinements": deploy-job isolation OD22, SQL stops ADR-0011, IAM-stack approvals OD32)
256	     4	- **Date:** 2026-11-09
257	     5	- **Decided by:** owner of this submission (OD8, OD11, OD13)
258	     6	- **Scope:** deploy workflows for Pulumi and Serverless stacks; k0s and Firebase not covered yet
259	     7	
260	     8	## 1. Context
261	     9	
262	    10	With the gate at merge time (ADR-0003), the approver reviews the code change, not the prod diff. A
263	    11	PR may not preview prod, because that would run PR code with state-write and secret access
264	    12	(📖 R4.3.3, R4.3.4; ⚠️ R4.6 #2). So a stateful delete or an IAM change can reach prod without anyone
265	    13	seeing its real effect. Most IAM, network and stateful changes sit inside domain files such as
266	    14	`serverless.yml`, not in separate L3 paths (assumed ⚠️; we have no access to the repo).
267	    15	
268	    16	## 2. Options considered
269	    17	
270	    18	| Option | Pros | Cons |
271	    19	|---|---|---|
272	    20	| A. Accept the gap | No extra step | Destructive diffs applied unseen |
273	    21	| B. Risk stop, approved by the L3 owner team | Specialist review | Often a third person; L3 team must be on call 24/7 |
274	    22	| C. Risk stop, approved by an owner of the stack | Stays at two people; works at night | Less specialist review; compensated by automated checks |
275	    23	
276	    24	## 3. Decision
277	    25	
278	    26	Option C [design]. The deploy job on `main` previews prod. On stateful replace/delete, an IAM
279	    27	change, a network or security-group change, or (from phase 2) an advisory policy finding, it stops
280	    28	and posts the filtered preview. The original author opens a PR (the workflow does not, as "Allow GitHub Actions to create and
281	    29	approve pull requests" stays off, 📖 R3.3.3; ⚠️ R3.6 #3) adding
282	    30	`deploy-approvals/<stack>/<sha>.yaml` with the SHA and preview hash (owned by the stack's owners and the
283	    31	on-call group, OD8, OD9); the first approver approves it
284	    32	(OD13). If that approver is unavailable, another stack owner approves; this makes three people and
285	    33	is recorded as a deviation (OD11). After the merge the workflow previews again on the new HEAD and
286	    34	continues only if the hash matches. Serverless uses `serverless diff --json` (sf-core ≥ 4.37.0), parsed by CI because
287	    35	differences do not change the exit code (📖 R4.4.2). A `mandatory` Pulumi policy violation always
288	    36	blocks `pulumi up` (📖 R4.2.2; policy packs from phase 2).
289	    37	
290	    38	## 4. Consequences
291	    39	
292	    40	- **Positive:** the person who approves now sees the prod diff for the changes that can do lasting
293	    41	  damage. Still two people in the normal case.
294	    42	- **Negative / trade-offs:** while a stack is stopped, later deploys to it stop too (the hash
295	    43	  differs), including an incident fix, until the approval lands or the change is reverted. One more review round when the stop fires.
296	    44	- **Risks & how we watch them:** preview output may not be stable enough to hash (⚠️ Options §8); if
297	    45	  not, compare a structured summary. Until phase 2, the risk stop is the only compensation for OD8;
298	    46	  Access Analyzer `check-no-new-access` (📖 R2.8.1) and policy packs follow. k0s and Firebase have no
299	    47	  preview step in this design (⚠️ G1, G2).
300	    48	- **Next steps:** risk stop in the deploy job in phase 1.
301	    49	
302	    50	## 5. References
303	    51	
304	    52	- Framework layer 3 ("Risk stop"), layer 5 (required checks); `work/03-options.md` §1.
305	    53	- Related: ADR-0001, ADR-0003.
306	=== docs/adr/0005-break-glass-is-time-limited-jit.md
307	     1	# ADR-0005: Break-glass is a time-limited, approved JIT grant, for incidents only
308	     2	
309	     3	- **Status:** Accepted
310	     4	- **Date:** 2026-11-09
311	     5	- **Decided by:** owner of this submission (GĐ-8; Options §9 Q2; D2; OD7, OD13)
312	     6	- **Scope:** AWS production accounts through IAM Identity Center; k0s and Firebase not covered (G1, G2)
313	     7	
314	     8	## 1. Context
315	     9	
316	    10	Some incidents cannot use the PR path: GitHub or Actions is down, the pipeline is broken, or the
317	    11	operation is not in IaC and has no runbook. Without a defined fallback, people keep standing access
318	    12	"just in case", which ADR-0002 removes.
319	    13	
320	    14	## 2. Options considered
321	    15	
322	    16	| Option | Pros | Cons |
323	    17	|---|---|---|
324	    18	| A. No fallback | Single path | Outage of GitHub blocks every fix; pressure to keep standing access |
325	    19	| B. Standing break-glass account, used first and approved later | Always available | Standing prod write; unapproved use, rejected by the owner (GĐ-8, Options §0.4) |
326	    20	| C. Approved JIT grant, 1-hour role session, command list, reconciled after | Approval before use; time-boxed; traceable | Approves a command list, not an applied change (partial) |
327	    21	
328	    22	## 3. Decision
329	    23	
330	    24	Option C [design], used only during an incident when the PR path cannot be used.
331	    25	
332	    26	- **Request:** command list, scope, reason, incident link, in a channel that does not depend on GitHub.
333	    27	- **Approval:** the on-call approver ≠ requester, before the grant; the on-call approver counts as
334	    28	  owner of the service (OD13).
335	    29	- **Grant:** `InfraOperator-<service>` [design name], assigned via `CreateAccountAssignment` and removed
336	    30	  via `DeleteAccountAssignment` (📖 R2.4.2); role session 1 h (📖 R2.1.4). *Refined by OD33:* a
337	    31	  receiver of the Linear webhook makes the grant only after checking approver ≠ requester, on
338	    32	  shift, open incident and the allowed set (examples E16), so the approval rule is enforced
339	    33	  before the grant, not only reviewed after it.
340	    34	- **Execution:** the incident responder types the commands in a terminal without an agent (D2, OD7).
341	    35	- **Example request** (illustrative command ⚠️): "INC-123, ECS service `claims-api`, Actions outage.
342	    36	  Run `aws ecs update-service --cluster <prod-cluster> --service <svc> --force-new-deployment`. Scope
343	    37	  `InfraOperator-claims`, 1 h."
344	    38	- **After:** CloudTrail writes in the window are compared with the list; a codify PR follows by a
345	    39	  fixed deadline; drift detection runs until it merges.
346	    40

356	    50	  Metrics: JIT used where a PR was possible, writes outside the list, late codify PRs (review at 1).

358	    52	  touched stacks in phase 1 (a temporary deviation from D2); revocation SCP and
359	    53	  automated reconciliation in phase 2.

367	     2	
368	     3	- **Status:** Accepted
369	     4	- **Date:** 2026-11-09
370	     5	- **Decided by:** owner of this submission (framework approval 2026-11-09; rollout priority framing Q8)
371	     6	- **Scope:** Claude Code on all engineer laptops and in CI; Papaya's internal plugin marketplace
372	     7	
373	     8	## 1. Context
374	     9	
375	    10	Local MCP servers, plugins and hooks run with the engineer's access (📖 R1.6.2, R5.5.5); remote MCP
376	    11	servers receive tokens and data. Papaya runs an internal plugin marketplace (brief, Appendix A), and
377	    12	engineers install MCP servers without review (brief); use of Linear and Slack through MCP is assumed
378	    13	(⚠️ G9). An unreviewed server or a plugin update can read the repo, the SSO cache or claim
379	    14	data and send it out.
380	    15	
381	    16	## 2. Options considered
382	    17	
383	    18	| Option | Pros | Cons |
384	    19	|---|---|---|
385	    20	| A. Free choice, guidance only | No friction | No inventory; any server can exfiltrate |
386	    21	| B. Denylist known-bad servers | Low friction | Misses new and changed servers |
387	    22	| C. Allowlist (catalogue) enforced by managed settings | Inventory and supplier records; blocks unknown servers | Up to 5 working days' wait for a new tool (S6) |
388	    23	
389	    24	## 3. Decision
390	    25	
391	    26	Option C. The catalogue is a file in git, changed by PR under the L3 owner team.
392	    27	
393	    28	- **Plugins:** only Papaya's marketplace via managed `strictKnownMarketplaces`, plus
394	    29	  `blockedMarketplaces` (📖 R1.4.2); sources pinned to `ref`/`sha` (📖 R1.4.1b, link only);
395	    30	  `disableSideloadFlags` (📖 R1.4.2); version floor covering the plugin-pin fix of 2.1.179 (📖 R6.2.7).
396	    31	- **MCP:** `allowedMcpServers` with `allowManagedMcpServersOnly: true` (📖 R1.3.1, R1.3.4); match by
397	    32	  `serverUrl` or `serverCommand` (exact argv), never `serverName`, which "is not a security control"
398	    33	  (📖 R1.3.3); `disableClaudeAiConnectors: true` (📖 R1.3.7).
399	    34	- **Review checklist** [design]: publisher, local or remote, what it reads and where it sends data,
400	    35	  supplier-register entry and BAA/DPA status, no token passthrough (📖 R6.4.2), pinned version.
401	    36	  Example entry: `serverCommand` = `["npx", "<package>@<exact-version>"]` [design; placeholder].
402	    37	- **CI:** server-managed settings do not reach a CI job (📖 R1.7.10); CI uses a managed-settings
403	    38	  file on the runner and a fixed MCP set, because `.mcp.json` loads without a prompt in `-p` runs
404	    39	  (📖 R1.3.5).
405	    40	
406	    41	## 4. Consequences
407	    42	
408	    43	- **Positive:** Compliance gets an asset inventory and supplier records (P4c); unknown servers are
409	    44	  refused before they load.
410	    45	- **Negative / trade-offs:** waiting time for new tools; review effort for 1–2 DevSecOps people.
411	    46	- **Risks & how we watch them:** the enforced copy lives in server-managed settings, edited in the
412	    47	  admin console by Owners, not by PR (📖 R1.1.5); an Owner exports and diffs it with git monthly until
413	    48	  G18 is solved (ADR-0007). `disableSideloadFlags` does not cover `.mcp.json` or `claude mcp add`
414	    49	  (📖 R1.4.2), so the MCP allowlist must be locked. No per-group targeting in server-managed settings
415	    50	  (📖 R1.1.6). Tool description changes after approval are not covered (⚠️). Without MDM, laptops can
416	    51	  bypass server-managed settings (📖 R1.1.7; ⚠️ G11). Evidence: OTel `plugin_installed` /
417	    52	  `plugin_loaded` (📖 R1.4.6).
418	    53	- **Next steps:** catalogue v1 in phase 1 (may slip to phase 2 only with owner agreement).
419	    54
